concept.name: Fork
concept.why: The knight on c7 forks the rook on a8 and the king on e8.
concept.wording: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
cautions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.

concepts.name: Knight fork
concepts.wording: A knight fork: one knight attacks two or more pieces, and neither interposition nor counter-attack defends, because a knight cannot be blocked and attacks the opposite colour to the one it occupies.
cautions: The landing square must be safe. This base's fork controlled pair shows the same knight move at +7.39 and at +0.57 depending only on whether one bishop guards the square.
A knight fork on a guarded square wins nothing.

concepts.name: Hanging piece
concepts.why: It leaves the rook on a8 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

altConcept.name: Pin
altConcept.why: The pawn on e2 is pinned to the king behind it and cannot step aside.
altConcept.wording: A pin. The pinned piece is stuck and makes a poor defender, so you can pile up on it.
cautions: A pinned piece still delivers check and still guards squares against non-king units.
A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concepts.name: Doubled pawns
concepts.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.

concepts.name: Restraint
concepts.wording: Restraint: preventing enemy pawns and pieces from advancing, as progress in its own right. It is the first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula — first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
cautions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.

concept.name: Check
concept.wording: Check: the king is attacked, and the side to move has exactly three ways to answer — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker. Nothing else is legal, which is why a check is the most forcing move there is.
cautions: A check being available is not a reason to play it. Proven case: Ra7+ draws and Rg8+ loses in the same position.
A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.

altConcept.name: Battery
altConcept.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.
